claim: CAMK2 comprises as much as 0.3% of the total brain protein content.
source: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CAMK2) is a calcium-activated serine/threonine kinase that is extremely abundant in the brain, comprising as much as 0.3% of the total brain protein content (Bennett et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bennett et al., 1983

claim: CAMK2 is highly enriched at the synapses.
source: CAMK2 is highly enriched at the synapses and is necessary for the process of long-term potentiation (LTP), the activity-dependent strengthening and modulation of synaptic activity that is thought to be the molecular basis of some forms of learning and memory (Kandel et al., 2014; Lisman et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kandel et al., 2014 and Lisman et al., 2002

claim: CAMK2 is necessary for the process of long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: CAMK2 is highly enriched at the synapses and is necessary for the process of long-term potentiation (LTP), the activity-dependent strengthening and modulation of synaptic activity that is thought to be the molecular basis of some forms of learning and memory (Kandel et al., 2014; Lisman et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kandel et al., 2014 and Lisman et al., 2002

claim: There are four genes encoding distinct CAMK2 iso-enzymes in humans.
source: In humans, there are four genes encoding distinct CAMK2 iso-enzymes.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about human CAMK2 genes

claim: CAMK2A and CAMK2B are the predominant isoforms in the nervous system.
source: CAMK2A and CAMK2B are the predominant isoforms in the nervous system, with CAMK2A being expressed 3–4 times higher than CAMK2B (Hanson and Schulman, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanson and Schulman, 1992

claim: CAMK2A is expressed 3–4 times higher than CAMK2B.
source: CAMK2A and CAMK2B are the predominant isoforms in the nervous system, with CAMK2A being expressed 3–4 times higher than CAMK2B (Hanson and Schulman, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanson and Schulman, 1992

claim: Each CAMK2 enzyme comprises a kinase domain, a regulatory domain and an association domain.
source: Each enzyme comprises a kinase domain, a regulatory domain and an association domain.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about CAMK2 structure

claim: CAMK2 holoenzymes are homo- or hetero-oligomers, consisting of 12 or 14 CAMK2 subunits.
source: Structurally CAMK2 holoenzymes are homo- or hetero-oligomers, consisting of 12 or 14 CAMK2 subunits (Hudmon and Schulman, 2002b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hudmon and Schulman, 2002b

claim: The holoenzyme assembly requires the carboxy-terminal association domain.
source: The holoenzyme assembly requires the carboxy-terminal association domain, which forms stacked pairs of hexameric or heptameric rings with the regulatory and kinase domain projecting radially to interact with other essential proteins for CAMK2 function and localization (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhattacharyya et al., 2016

claim: In the absence of calcium signalling, CAMK2 is inactive, as the regulatory domain inhibits kinase function.
source: In the absence of calcium signalling, CAMK2 is inactive, as the regulatory domain inhibits kinase function (Yang and Schulman, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang and Schulman, 1999

claim: Auto-inhibition of CAMK2 is relieved when calcium-loaded calmodulin binds to the regulatory domain.
source: This auto-inhibition is relieved when calcium-loaded calmodulin binds to the regulatory domain, thereby exposing the kinase domain and allowing it to phosphorylate target substrates (Meador et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meador et al., 1993

claim: Ca2+-Calmodulin binding exposes Thr286 on the regulatory domain of CAMK2A.
source: Ca2+-Calmodulin binding also exposes Thr286 on the regulatory domain of CAMK2A, which becomes phosphorylated in trans by adjacent subunits.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about CAMK2A mechanism

claim: Once Thr286 is phosphorylated, the CAMK2A enzyme is persistently active, even in the absence of continual Ca2+-Calmodulin signaling.
source: Once this residue is phosphorylated, the enzyme is persistently active, even in the absence of continual Ca2+-Calmodulin signaling (Rich and Schulman, 1998; Stratton et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rich and Schulman, 1998 and Stratton et al., 2013

claim: The switch from auto-inhibition to autonomous, persistent activity is thought to constitute a biochemical form of memory.
source: This switch from auto-inhibition to autonomous, persistent activity is thought to constitute a biochemical form of memory, which marks the neuron for having experienced a previous calcium influx (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016; Stratton et al., 2014; Stratton et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhattacharyya et al., 2016, Stratton et al., 2014, and Stratton et al., 2013

claim: Mice that are homozygous null for CAMK2A are viable.
source: Mice that are homozygous null for CAMK2A are viable and display impaired spatial memory and reduced LTP in the hippocampus (Silva et al., 1992a, 1992b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Silva et al., 1992a and 1992b

claim: Mice that are homozygous null for CAMK2A display impaired spatial memory and reduced LTP in the hippocampus.
source: Mice that are homozygous null for CAMK2A are viable and display impaired spatial memory and reduced LTP in the hippocampus (Silva et al., 1992a, 1992b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Silva et al., 1992a and 1992b

claim: Heterozygous Camk2a+/- mice show a significant deficit in spatial working memory and contextual fear memory.
source: The heterozygous mutant (Camk2a+/-) show a significant deficit in spatial working memory and contextual fear memory (Frankland et al., 2001; Matsuo et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frankland et al., 2001 and Matsuo et al., 2009

claim: Mice with neuron-specific conditional knock-out of CAMK2A displayed learning deficits and defects in LTP comparable to complete knockout mice.
source: More recently, it was demonstrated that mice with neuron-specific conditional knock-out of CAMK2A similarly displayed learning deficits and defects in LTP that were comparable to the complete knockout mice (Achterberg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Achterberg et al., 2014

claim: Neuron-intrinsic CAMK2A function is indispensable during the period of learning for memory formation.
source: These findings suggest that neuron-intrinsic CAMK2A function is indispensable during the period of learning for memory formation.
evidence: Inferred from the cited mouse studies

claim: CAMK2 is conserved in invertebrates, such as D. melanogaster and C. elegans.
source: CAMK2 is conserved in invertebrates, such as D. melanogaster and C. elegans, where the kinase also plays critical roles in behavioral and cognitive traits (Cho et al., 1991; Hudmon and Schulman, 2002a; Reiner et al., 1999; Rongo and Kaplan, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cho et al., 1991, Hudmon and Schulman, 2002a, Reiner et al., 1999, and Rongo and Kaplan, 1999

claim: In C. elegans, the only CAMK2 is encoded by the unc-43 gene.
source: In C. elegans, the only CAMK2 is encoded by the unc-43 gene, which is essential for synaptic function (Rongo and Kaplan, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rongo and Kaplan, 1999

claim: unc-43 is essential for synaptic function in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, the only CAMK2 is encoded by the unc-43 gene, which is essential for synaptic function (Rongo and Kaplan, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rongo and Kaplan, 1999

claim: Loss of unc-43 causes worms to have flaccid muscle tone, locomotion defects and spontaneous body contractions that resemble seizures.
source: Loss of unc-43 causes worms to have flaccid muscle tone, locomotion defects and spontaneous body contractions that resemble seizures (Reiner et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reiner et al., 1999

claim: Global developmental delay in infants is defined as a significant functional delay in two or more developmental domains.
source: In pediatric care, global developmental delay in infants is defined as a significant functional delay in two or more developmental domains including gross and fine motor function, speech and language, cognition, social development and personal skills (Quality Standards Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quality Standards Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology et al., 2003

claim: About 25–50% of identified cases of global developmental delay are caused by germline genetic changes.
source: About 25–50% of identified case are caused by germline genetic changes, including chromosomal abnormalities, copy number variants and monogenic mutations (Srour and Shevell, 2014; van Bokhoven, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Srour and Shevell, 2014 and van Bokhoven, 2011

claim: A consanguineous family from Jordan has two affected children manifesting global neuro-developmental delay with frequent seizures and convulsions.
source: Here, we report the identification of a consanguineous family from Jordan with two affected children manifesting global neuro-developmental delay with frequent seizures and convulsions.
evidence: Clinical observation reported in the manuscript

claim: The two affected siblings had no dysmorphic features.
source: The two affected siblings had no dysmorphic features but failed to develop the ability to walk or speak (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Clinical observation supported by figures showing patient photographs

claim: The two affected siblings failed to develop the ability to walk or speak.
source: The two affected siblings had no dysmorphic features but failed to develop the ability to walk or speak (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Clinical observation supported by clinical data table in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The affected siblings displayed progressive psychomotor retardation with hypotonic muscles.
source: They displayed progressive psychomotor retardation with hypotonic muscles (Supplemental Material, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Clinical observation supported by videos

claim: EEG analysis revealed abnormal epileptiform transients in the affected siblings.
source: Electroencephalogram (EEG) analysis revealed abnormal epileptiform transients (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), consistent with frequent myoclonic seizures.
evidence: EEG data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: MRI scan showed no major structural defects in the brain of proband II:4.
source: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan showed no major structural defects in the brain of proband II:4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: MRI images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Serum metabolite levels were normal in the affected siblings.
source: Serum metabolite levels were normal, ruling out potential lysosomal storage disorders.
evidence: Clinical test results reported in the manuscript

claim: Identity-by-descent homozygosity mapping delineated one candidate locus greater than 5 cM on chromosome 5 spanning 28 Mb.
source: Only one candidate locus greater than 5 cM on chromosome 5 spanning 28 Mb was delineated (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Homozygosity mapping data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Whole-exome sequencing identified 72 homozygous variants after filtering for variants with low quality and low sequencing coverage.
source: After filtering for variants with low quality and low sequencing coverage, 72 homozygous variants were identified, out of which four lie within the Chr. 5 IBD region (Table 1).
evidence: Exome sequencing data presented in Table 1

claim: Four homozygous variants lie within the Chr. 5 IBD region.
source: After filtering for variants with low quality and low sequencing coverage, 72 homozygous variants were identified, out of which four lie within the Chr. 5 IBD region (Table 1).
evidence: Exome sequencing data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: Three of the homozygous variants within the Chr. 5 IBD region had been previously annotated as known polymorphisms with minor allele frequencies > 0.0001.
source: Three of the homozygous variants had been previously annotated as known polymorphisms with minor allele frequencies > 0.0001.
evidence: Comparison with genomic databases

claim: The fourth homozygous variant within the IBD region mapped to the CAMK2A gene, resulting in a missense mutation p.His477Tyr.
source: The fourth homozygous variant within the IBD region mapped to the CAMK2A gene (MIM: 114078), resulting in a missense mutation p.His477Tyr that has never been observed in previous large-scale sequencing databases and our in-house ethnically-matched cohort (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Exome sequencing data and database comparison

claim: The p.His477Tyr mutation has never been observed in previous large-scale sequencing databases and in-house ethnically-matched cohort.
source: The fourth homozygous variant within the IBD region mapped to the CAMK2A gene (MIM: 114078), resulting in a missense mutation p.His477Tyr that has never been observed in previous large-scale sequencing databases and our in-house ethnically-matched cohort (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Comparison with genomic databases and in-house cohort

claim: The p.His477Tyr mutation segregates with the disease in all seven family members.
source: Using Sanger sequencing, this private mutation was confirmed to segregate with the disease in all seven family members (Figure 1A,D).
evidence: Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1A,D

claim: The p.H477Y mutation is located in the CAMK2A association domain.
source: The identified mutation, p.H477Y is located in the association domain (Figure 1E) and affects a histidine residue that is invariant across all vertebrate and invertebrate CAMK2A homologues.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1E depicting CAMK2A protein domains

claim: His477 is invariant across all vertebrate and invertebrate CAMK2A homologues.
source: The identified mutation, p.H477Y is located in the association domain (Figure 1E) and affects a histidine residue that is invariant across all vertebrate and invertebrate CAMK2A homologues.
evidence: Sequence conservation analysis

claim: His477 is conserved in other human CAMK2 paralogs with a similar association domain such as CAMK2B, CAMK2D and CAMK2G.
source: It is also conserved in other human CAMK2 paralogs with a similar association domain such as CAMK2B, CAMK2D and CAMK2G (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Sequence alignment shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The p.H477Y mutation is predicted to be deleterious by SIFT, PolyPhen and MCAP algorithms.
source: In addition, this mutation is predicted to be deleterious by both SIFT, PolyPhen and MCAP algorithms.
evidence: Computational prediction algorithms

claim: His477 is located at the dimeric interface that forms part of the extensive interaction surface at the 'equatorial' plane of the CAMK2A holoenzyme.
source: Structurally, His477 is located at the dimeric interface that forms part of the extensive interaction surface at the 'equatorial' plane of the CAMK2A holoenzyme (Figure 3B).
evidence: Structural analysis shown in Figure 3B using X-ray crystal structure

claim: Patient-derived iPSCs were equally efficient in differentiating into mature neurons expressing neuronal markers TUJ1 and MAP2 after 21 days of in vitro differentiation compared to controls.
source: Compared to H1 embryonic stem cell derived neurons and an unrelated CAMK2A wild-type iPSC control, the patient's iPSCs were equally efficient in differentiating into mature neurons expressing neuronal markers TUJ1 and MAP2 after 21 days of in vitro differentiation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Patient-derived neurons harboring the p.H477Y mutation showed a significant reduction in the total number of spontaneous spikes compared to wild-type controls.
source: When these differentiated neurons were plated on MEA plates to measure spontaneous action potentials, we observed a significant reduction in both the total number of spontaneous spikes (Figure 2C, left) and the mean firing rate (Figure 2C, right) in the patient-derived neurons harboring the p.H477Y mutation compared to the wild-type controls, suggesting that CAMK2AH477Y causes a profound functional defect in cultured neurons.
evidence: Multi-electrode array data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Patient-derived neurons harboring the p.H477Y mutation showed a significant reduction in the mean firing rate compared to wild-type controls.
source: When these differentiated neurons were plated on MEA plates to measure spontaneous action potentials, we observed a significant reduction in both the total number of spontaneous spikes (Figure 2C, left) and the mean firing rate (Figure 2C, right) in the patient-derived neurons harboring the p.H477Y mutation compared to the wild-type controls, suggesting that CAMK2AH477Y causes a profound functional defect in cultured neurons.
evidence: Multi-electrode array data shown in Figure 2C

claim: CAMK2AH477Y causes a profound functional defect in cultured neurons.
source: When these differentiated neurons were plated on MEA plates to measure spontaneous action potentials, we observed a significant reduction in both the total number of spontaneous spikes (Figure 2C, left) and the mean firing rate (Figure 2C, right) in the patient-derived neurons harboring the p.H477Y mutation compared to the wild-type controls, suggesting that CAMK2AH477Y causes a profound functional defect in cultured neurons.
evidence: Inferred from MEA data showing reduced neuronal activity

claim: Wild-type CAMK2A forms a prominent complex with an apparent molecular weight ~1 MDa.
source: Using native lysis conditions that preserve non-covalent macromolecular interactions, we found that wild-type CAMK2A forms a prominent complex with an apparent molecular weight ~1 MDa (Figure 3C, Native-PAGE, lane 2), which is consistent with the 12- or 14- subunit CAMK2A holoenzyme (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: Native-PAGE data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The ~1 MDa oligomeric species was drastically reduced for the p.H477Y mutant compared to wild-type CAMK2A.
source: As compared to wild-type CAMK2A, the ~1 MDa, putatively oligomeric species was drastically reduced for the p.H477Y mutant and was undetectable for the p.H477X mutant (Figure 3C, Native-PAGE, lane 3 and 4 vs. lane 2).
evidence: Native-PAGE data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The ~1 MDa oligomeric species was undetectable for the p.H477X mutant.
source: As compared to wild-type CAMK2A, the ~1 MDa, putatively oligomeric species was drastically reduced for the p.H477Y mutant and was undetectable for the p.H477X mutant (Figure 3C, Native-PAGE, lane 3 and 4 vs. lane 2).
evidence: Native-PAGE data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Wild-type FLAG-CAMK2A efficiently co-immunoprecipitated with HA-CAMK2A.
source: In contrast to the negative control protein GFP, wild-type FLAG-CAMK2A efficiently co-immunoprecipitated with HA-CAMK2A (Figure 3D, Lane 10 vs 11).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Self-association was preserved between CAMK2AWT and CAMK2AH477Y.
source: This self-association was preserved between CAMK2AWT and CAMK2AH477Y (Figure 3D, lanes 12 and 15), but was completely lost between wild-type CAMK2A and the p.H477X mutant (Figure 3D, lane 13).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Self-association was completely lost between wild-type CAMK2A and the p.H477X mutant.
source: This self-association was preserved between CAMK2AWT and CAMK2AH477Y (Figure 3D, lanes 12 and 15), but was completely lost between wild-type CAMK2A and the p.H477X mutant (Figure 3D, lane 13).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D

claim: No self-association was detected between FLAG-CAMK2AH477Y and HA-CAMK2AH477Y.
source: In contrast, we could not detect any self-association between FLAG- CAMK2AH477Y and HA- CAMK2AH477Y (Figure 3D, Lane 16).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The p.H477Y mutation partially disrupts the self-association between identical CAMK2A molecules.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the missense p.H477Y partially disrupts the self-association between identical CAMK2A molecules, which had been shown to be required for holoenzyme assembly.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation experiments

claim: Both p.H477Y and p.H477X mutants had reduced protein abundance.
source: During the course of this analysis, we noticed that both p.H477Y and p.H477X mutants had reduced protein abundance.
evidence: Observed in protein expression experiments

claim: A significant reduction in GFP intensity was observed in cells expressing CAMK2AH477Y and CAMK2AH477X as compared to wild-type CAMK2A or GFP alone.
source: We observed a significant reduction in GFP intensity in cells expressing CAMK2AH477Y and CAMK2AH477X as compared to wild-type CAMK2A or GFP alone (Figure 3E) despite comparable mCherry fluorescence levels.
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3E

claim: MG132 treatment led to enhanced accumulation of the p.H477Y and p.H477X mutant.
source: MG132 treamentled to enhanced accumulation of the p.H477Y and p.H477X mutant, with a greater effect on p.H477X (Figure 3F, lane 3, 4 vs lane 7, 8, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The p.H477Y mutation reduces the overall CAMK2A levels by compromising its half-life.
source: These results suggest that in addition to causing reduced holoenzyme assembly, the p.H477Y mutation might also directly or indirectly reduce the overall CAMK2A levels by compromising its half-life.
evidence: Inferred from MG132 rescue experiments

claim: UNC-43 is concentrated at synaptic boutons in DA9 neurons.
source: Using mCherry-tagged UNC-43, we observed that UNC-43 could be found along the entire DA9 neuron but concentrated at synaptic boutons (Figure 4B).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The homologous patient-specific mutation p.H466Y in UNC-43 significantly disrupted the synaptic localization of UNC-43.
source: The homologous patient-specific mutation p.H466Y in UNC-43 (homologous to p.H477Y in human CAMK2A) significantly disrupted the synaptic localization of UNC-43 and caused the protein to be dispersed throughout the entire axon (Figure 4B).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B

claim: In the unc-43(e408) loss-of-function mutant, a reduction in individual pre-synaptic puncta fluorescence intensity was observed compared to wild-type animals.
source: In the canonical unc-43(e408) loss-of-function mutant, we observed a reduction in individual pre-synaptic puncta fluorescence intensity as compared to wild-type animals.
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy quantification

claim: Cell-autonomous expression of wild-type unc-43 in DA9 rescued the pre-synaptic puncta defect in unc-43(e408) mutants.
source: This phenotype could be rescued by cell-autonomous expression of wild-type unc-43 in DA9. However, expression of unc-43 harboring the homologous patient mutation UNC-43H466Y failed to rescue this defect (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: Expression of unc-43 harboring the homologous patient mutation UNC-43H466Y failed to rescue the pre-synaptic puncta defect in unc-43(e408) mutants.
source: This phenotype could be rescued by cell-autonomous expression of wild-type unc-43 in DA9. However, expression of unc-43 harboring the homologous patient mutation UNC-43H466Y failed to rescue this defect (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: Transgenic expression of human wild-type CAMK2A fully rescued the pre-synaptic puncta defect in unc-43(e408) mutants.
source: In addition, transgenic expression of human wild-type CAMK2A fully rescued this defect, confirming the high degree of functional conservation between CAMK2A homologs, while the patient-derived human CAMK2AH477Y failed to do so (Figure 4C, bottom panels).
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The patient-derived human CAMK2AH477Y failed to rescue the pre-synaptic puncta defect in unc-43(e408) mutants.
source: In addition, transgenic expression of human wild-type CAMK2A fully rescued this defect, confirming the high degree of functional conservation between CAMK2A homologs, while the patient-derived human CAMK2AH477Y failed to do so (Figure 4C, bottom panels).
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The p.H477Y mutation is defective in supporting pre-synaptic function in C. elegans.
source: These results suggest that the p.H477Y mutation is defective in supporting pre-synaptic function in C. elegans.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments in C. elegans

claim: Loss of unc-43 results in the mislocalization of the synaptic marker RAB3::GFP into the asynaptic region.
source: Immediately posterior to the stretch of presynaptic puncta is an asynaptic domain within the DA9 axon that is devoid of any RAB-3::GFP fluorescence in wild-type animals (Figure 4E, top panel). Loss of unc-43 results in the mislocalization of the synaptic marker RAB3::GFP into this asynaptic region (Figure 4E, bottom panel).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Cell autonomous expression of either unc-43 or human CAMK2A rescued the RAB3::GFP mislocalization defect in unc-43 mutants.
source: This defect could also be rescued by cell autonomous expression of either unc-43 or human CAMK2A. Patient derived mutation CAMK2AH477Y or the worm homologous mutation UNC-43H466Y both failed to rescue this phenotype (Figure 4E).
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Patient derived mutation CAMK2AH477Y or the worm homologous mutation UNC-43H466Y both failed to rescue the RAB3::GFP mislocalization phenotype.
source: This defect could also be rescued by cell autonomous expression of either unc-43 or human CAMK2A. Patient derived mutation CAMK2AH477Y or the worm homologous mutation UNC-43H466Y both failed to rescue this phenotype (Figure 4E).
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Expression of UNC-43H466Y in wild-type animals did not cause any synaptic defect or mislocalization of RAB3::GFP.
source: In addition, expression of UNC-43H466Y in wild-type animals did not cause any synaptic defect or mislocalizaton of RAB3::GFP, suggesting that the mutation does not have dominant negative effects (Figure 4F).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The UNC-43H466Y mutation does not have dominant negative effects.
source: In addition, expression of UNC-43H466Y in wild-type animals did not cause any synaptic defect or mislocalizaton of RAB3::GFP, suggesting that the mutation does not have dominant negative effects (Figure 4F).
evidence: Inferred from lack of phenotype in wild-type background

claim: Null mutants for unc-43 are flaccid in posture and move with a flattened uncoordinated waveform.
source: Null mutants for unc-43 are flaccid in posture and move with a flattened uncoordinated waveform.
evidence: Behavioral observation of unc-43 mutants

claim: unc-43 mutant animals are variably convulsive, often spontaneously contracting and relaxing their body-wall muscles in brief repeating bursts that resemble seizures.
source: The animals are variably convulsive, often spontaneously contracting and relaxing their body-wall muscles in brief repeating bursts that resemble seizures (Reiner et al., 1999).
evidence: Behavioral observation supported by citation to Reiner et al., 1999

claim: Only wild-type UNC-43 was able to rescue the movement defects in unc-43(e408) animals, but not UNC-43H466Y.
source: Only the wildtype UNC-43 was able to rescue the movement defects in unc-43(e408) animals, but not UNC-43H466Y, suggesting that UNC-43H466Y is not functional (Figure 4G).
evidence: Behavioral rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4G

claim: UNC-43H466Y is not functional.
source: Only the wildtype UNC-43 was able to rescue the movement defects in unc-43(e408) animals, but not UNC-43H466Y, suggesting that UNC-43H466Y is not functional (Figure 4G).
evidence: Inferred from failure to rescue behavioral defects

claim: CAMK2AH477Y is a loss-of-function mutation which fails to support synaptic function in vivo.
source: Together, the data show that CAMK2AH477Y is a loss-of-function mutation which fails to support synaptic function in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from all C. elegans rescue experiments

claim: An autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by growth delay, frequent seizures and severe intellectual disability is caused by a biallelic germline loss-of-function mutation in CAMK2A.
source: In summary, we have identified an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by growth delay, frequent seizures and severe intellectual disability that is caused by a biallelic germline loss-of-function mutation in CAMK2A.
evidence: Summary of all findings in the manuscript

claim: The p.H477Y mutation disrupts CAMK2A self-oligomerization and holoenzyme assembly via its association domain.
source: Mechanistically this mutation disrupts CAMK2A self-oligomerization and holoenzyme assembly via its association domain.
evidence: Demonstrated through biochemical experiments

claim: His477 is located in the interface between two stacked CAMK2A subunits, which together form the basic repeat unit of the ring-shaped holoenzyme.
source: Our functional results are consistent with the high degree of evolutionary conservation of the affected residue H477 in CAMK2A orthologs, as well as previous structural data demonstrating that His477 is located in the interface between two stacked CAMK2A subunits, which together form the basic repeat unit of the ring-shaped holoenzyme (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016; Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhattacharyya et al., 2016 and Stratton et al., 2014

claim: The loss of function of CAMK2A is the most plausible genetic cause for the neurodevelopmental defects observed in the two affected siblings.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the loss of function of CAMK2A is the most plausible genetic cause for the neurodevelopmental defects observed in the two affected siblings.
evidence: Inferred from all genetic, biochemical, and functional data

claim: A de novo p.E183V mutation in the CAMK2A catalytic domain was shown to cause autism spectrum disorder.
source: Notably, a de novo p.E183V mutation in the CAMK2A catalytic domain was shown to cause autism spectrum disorder (Stephenson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephenson et al., 2017

claim: The p.E183V mutation acts in a dominant-negative manner to reduce wild-type CAMK2A auto-phosphorylation and localization to dendritic spines.
source: This mutation was shown to act in a dominant-negative manner to reduce wild-type CAMK2A auto-phosphorylation and localization to dendritic spines.
evidence: Stated as established finding from prior research

claim: Multiple families with intellectual disability are caused by de novo, heterozygous mutations in both CAMK2A and CAMK2B kinase and auto-regulatory domains.
source: While this manuscript was under revision, S. Küry et al. reported multiple families with intellectual disability caused by de novo, heterozygous mutations in both CAMK2A and CAMK2B kinase and auto-regulatory domains, which disrupted CAMK2 phosphorylation and caused neuronal migratory defects in murine models (Küry et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Küry et al., 2017

claim: This represents the first Mendelian human disease caused by biallelic CAMK2A mutations.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first Mendelian human disease caused by biallelic CAMK2A mutations.
evidence: Stated as novel finding based on literature review

claim: The p.H477Y allele is hypomorphic and becomes pathogenic when recessively inherited in the homozygous state.
source: These biochemical results provide a mechanistic basis for the autosomal recessive nature of the disease in our family: the p.H477Y allele is hypomorphic and becomes pathogenic when recessively inherited in the homozygous state.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical characterization and inheritance pattern

claim: Heterozygous carriers of the p.H477Y allele retain sufficient CAMK2A activity for proper neuronal function.
source: We speculate that heterozygous carriers retain sufficient CAMK2A activity for proper neuronal function.
evidence: Speculated based on recessive inheritance pattern and lack of symptoms in carriers

claim: The symptoms afflicting the p.H477Y patients likely represent the most severe manifestation of the CAMK2A dysfunction in humans.
source: As compared to the milder disease phenotypes reported by Kury et. al., the symptoms afflicting the p.H477Y patients likely represent the most severe manifestation of the CAMK2A dysfunction in humans.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with other reported CAMK2A mutations
